                 ACCESS TO "‘ATTORNEY’S EYES ONLY” INFORMATION




        The Alliance for Aﬂbrdable Energy and the Union of Concerned Scientists (together,


‘-‘NPOs”) respectfully move for the Tribunal to grant the NPOS leave to reply to Entergy

Louisiana, LLC’s   i(“ELL”) Memorandum in Opposition to the Motion of the NPOs
(“Opposition”) ﬁled on June 24, 2025. The NPOs’ reply is attached to this Motion. In support of

this motion, the NPOs state:



        1. On July 15, 2026, the NPOS ﬁled a motion requesting that the Tribunal direct ELL to


provide the NPOS’ client representatives with access to conﬁdential information that ELL had

designated as “Attomeys Eyes Only” (AEO).


        2. On July 15, 2026, the Tribunal issued a Notice directing that any response to this


motion be ﬁled by July 17, 2026. The Notice did not provide for _any replies to the responses.



        3. On July 17, 2026, ELL ﬁled an Opposition to the NPO’s Motion.
        4. The NPOS seek leave to ﬁle a reply to ELL’s Opposition so that it can bring to the


Tribunal’s attention: a) ELL’s failure to address. the Tribunal’s previous determination in Docket

No. U-37425 regarding ELL’s ability to deny access to the NPOS; b) the concerns “supporting”


the AEO designation in the Conﬁdentiality Agreement do not justify denying AEO designated


infonnation to client representatives; c) ELL’s failure to correctly inform parties   regarding which
individuals are denied access to AEO information; cl) ELL’s desire to hide conﬁdential


infonnation from intervenors should not trump those intervenors’ right to fully participate in this


case; and e) preventing intervenors from reviewing AEO information is demonstrably


unnecessary as demonstrated by the NPOS’ participation in Docket No. U-3 7425 and the NPOS’


receipt and treatment of conﬁdential information in that proceeding.


       ELL’s conclusory statements should not be relied upon by the Tribunal in considering this


matter. Moreover, ELL’s failure to address applicable precedent, and failure to support the need

for the AEO designation should be considered by the Tribunal in reaching a decision on this


matter. The attached Reply Memorandum is necessary to clarify the legal and factual issues


raised in ELL’s Opposition and will not unduly delay the Tribunal’s consideration of the Motion.



       WHEREFORE, the NPOs respectfully move for leave to reply to ELL’s Opposition.

                BEFORE THE LOUISIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION


 ENTERGY LOUISIANA LLC, ex parte


 IN RE: APPLICATION FOR

 APPROVAL OF GENERATION AND
                                                   DOCKET NO. U-37882
 TRANSl\/IISSION RESOURCES AND
 FOR OTHER RELIEF PURSUANT TO

 THE COMMISSION’S LIGHTWING

 INITIATI VF




          REPLY IN SUPPORT OF THE ALLIANCE FOR AFFORDABLE ENERGY AND
                      UNION OF CONCERNED SCIENTISTS.’ MOTION FOR
                    ACCESS TO “ATTORNEY"S EYES ONLY” INFORNIATION




         In their Motion for Access to “Attomey’s Eyes Only” Information (“Motion”), the Non-


Profit Organizations (“NPOS”), consisting of the Alliance for Affordable Energy (“Alliance”) and


Union of Concerned Scientists (“UCS”), have asked this Public Service Commission


(“Commission” or “LPSC”) to direct Entergy Louisiana, LLC (“ELL” or “Company”) to provide

their client representatives with access to information that ELL has designated as
                                                                                     “Attorney’s
Eyes Only” (“AEO”). As the NPOs explained,_ their client representatives should be given access

to this “AEO” material so that the NPOS may meaningfully participate in the examination of



pertinent materials-, submission ofpre-filed testimony, review of testimony submitted by other

parties, evidentiary hearing, and preparation of post-hearing briefs, and as Well as any settlement

discussions. The NPOs also explained that ELL’s refusal to provide the client representatives


with this information interferes with undersigned counsel’s ability to represent these clients. In


the Motion, NPOs expressly discuss that the issue of NPOs access to AEO designated material


Was   previously resolved in U-37425.
         Nothing in ELL’s, Opposition Memoranduml undercuts the points raised in the NPOS’

Motion. ELL fails to even mention the precedent set by the Tribunal in Docket No. U-3 7425 and


thereby fails to distinguish that Tribunal’s resolution of the matter in that proceeding. Moreover,

ELL fails to justify prohibiting only certain parties from reviewing the information at issue.


Furthermore, ELL’s concerns “supporting” the AEO designation in the Conﬁdentiality

Agreement do not justiﬁ denying AEO designated information to client representatives. These

justifications are particularly vital where, as here, application of the AEO designation denies

parties their right to fully participate in the proceeding and denies their right to counsel: The

NPOS’ receipt ofAEO designated information in Docket No. U-37425 and their appropriate


treatment of that information during that proceeding demonstrates that preventing the NPO client



representatives ﬁ‘om reviewing the'AEO designed information is wholly unnecessary to protect

that information from public release. Finally, ELL’s cavalier attitude toward informing all parties


which individuals cannot receive AEO information belies their assertion that the designation is


necessary to protect conﬁdential information.


       The arguments in ELL’s. Opposition are Without merit. _For the reasons further explained


below, the Tribunal should reject ELL’s arguments, and direct the Company to provide the NPO

client representatives with access to material that has been designated “Attorney’s Eyes Only.”




1
  Entergy Louisiana, LLC’s Memorandum in Opposition to Motion of the Alliance for Affordable
Energy and Union of"Concerned Scientists for Access to “Attorney’s Eyes Only” Information
(“Opposition”).
                                                  ARGUMENT



             A. ELL Failed to Mention, Let Alone Distinguish, the Tribunal 3' Decision in U-3 7425


             As the Tribunal is no doubt aware, ELL previously attempted to deny the NPOs access to


    AEO designated information in U-37425. The NPOs ﬁled a motion in that proceeding, similar to


    the Motion     at issue here, requesting that ELL provide AEO designated information to the NPOs.

    The Tribunal found that “disparate treatment is unwarranted” and ordered ELL to give the NPOs


    access to the AEO    designated materials?

             In ELL’s Opposition, the Company studiously fails to recognize the implications of this


    precedent. ELL fails to present any argument justifying the disparate treatment in this

    proceeding. Particularly since both proceedings are factually similar (both involve the

    construction of new combined.-cycle gas generation to serve a new hyperscale data center


    sponsored by Meta, and the ﬁlings contain allegedly commercially sensitive information), ELL

    was obligated to explain why disparate treatment is now warranted when that treatment was



    found to be unwarranted previously.


             The language in the Conﬁdentiality Agreement governing the AEO designation


    demonstrates that the disparate treatment remains unwarranted. Section 1.e states that this


    designation is needed because disclosure to any person other than Authorized Persons would.

    threaten substantial competitive or other harm. This phrasing is repeated twice in section 1.e.


    Section 2.c ‘provides speciﬁcs for the term “unreasonable harm”, deﬁning such harms as created


    by disclosure to persons whose duties include:

             (i)     the marketing or sale of electric power or energy at wholesale,




'

    2
        Docket No. U-37425, Ruling on Motion for Access to Attomey’s Eyes Only Information (June
    30, 2025).
           (ii)     the purchase or sale of electric power or energy at wholesale,

          (iii)    the provision of electricity marketing consulting services to entities engaged in
                   the -sale or purchase of electric power at wholesale;

          (iv)     the pricing for the sale of potential electric generation development project
                   facilities or the electric power or energy therefrom, or of potential upgrades or
                   enhancements to such facilities or the electric power or energy therefrom, with the
                   exception of the development and/or evaluation of proj ects for se_lf- or co-
                   generation of electricity;

          (V)      the pricing for competitive bids for purchases, sales, or construction of electric
                   transmission facilities; and

          (vi) design, construction, or operation of a data center.

         None     of these risks of harm apply to either the Alliance3 or UCS.4 ELL’s irrational

justification for denying NPOs’access to AEO designated information, is apparently that NPOS

cannot be trusted with public information because these organizations have the temerity to



publicly discuss and criticize public aspects of the application. Importantly, the NPOs have never

disclosed conﬁdential information to the public, While both ELL and Sierra Club5 have.


          Tellingly, the overwhelming majority of individuals denied access to AEO designated

information are the client representatives of the NPOs.6 The assumption that the AEO


designation was created largely, or even solely, to deny NPOS access to this informationwould

not be unreasonable. The protection from disparate treatment espoused in the precedent




    As described in its Motion to Intervene, the Alliance is a non-proﬁt organization that serves as
3


a consumer advocate for the electric      ratepayers of Louisiana, with special concern for residential
and small commercial customers. The Alliance is dedicated to supporting equitable, aﬁbrdable,
and environmentally responsible energy policy for the citizens ofLouisiana.
4
    UCS is a leading science-based advocacy nonproﬁt with more than half a million supporters
nationwide, including more than 1,000 in Louisiana. UCS puts rigorous, independent science
into action, developing solutions and advocating for a healthy, safe, and just future.
5
    Sierra Club ’s Motion to Intervene was removed from the public docket in this proceeding
because the document included HSPM infonnation.
6
    The only other individuals denied access to AEO designated information despite executing the

Conﬁdentiality Agreement are two client representatives of Southern Renewable Energy
Association (“SREA”).
 established in Docket No. U-37425 clearly is applicable to the current situation. ELL relies on


the same previously rejected allegations of “harm” to deny the NPOs access to conﬁdential


information in this proceeding. ELL’.s use of conﬁdentiality designations as a bludgeon to


prevent full participation by disfavored parties is patently unwarranted and should be prevented

by the Tribunal.




          B.   ELLsApplication of the “Attomeyis Eyes Only” Designation to All NPO Client
               Representatives is Prejudicial to those Organizations.

          The prejudice experienced in the application of the AEO designation stems ﬁ'orn the NPO


client representatives themselves being denied access to this material.            Restricting the client

representatives’ access to AEO material interferes with the NPOs’ attorney-client relationship.

Providing the client representatives with access to the AEO materials is necessary to the NPOS’

effective participation as intervenors in this case. As intervenors, the ,NPOs are full parties with a


demonstrated interest in this case.7 And although the NPOS are represented by counsel, the


client representatives, who    are   directly employed by the‘ Alliance for Affordable Energy and the

Union of Concerned Scientists, are the NPOS’ ultimate decisionmakers.                Restricting their access

to the AEO material renders the NPOS’ ability to participate in this case "almost non-existent.


          The fact that the NPOS’ counsel can View the information does not mitigate this prejudice


and the effect of applying the AEO designation is to deny the NPOs their right to counsel.8‘In


this regard, it is important to note that ELL has applied the “AEO” label to an extremely broad




7
    See LPSC Rule 1.0.
8
    See Louisiana Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.2(a) (“[A] lawyer shall abide by a client’s
decisions concerning the objectives of representation, and, as required by Rule 1.4, shall consult
with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued.     .   .   .
                                                                                 A lawyer shall abide by a
client’s decision whether to settle a matter.’’).
 swath of the record.   This is not a situation Where a utility selectively applied heightened

protections to a handﬁil of unusually sensitive data; ~ELL has categorized hundreds of pages of its

ﬁlings as “Attorney’s Eyes Only.” Moreover, much of the material labeled AEO is not even

“data” at all; ELL applied the AEO designation to, among other things:


0   The entire Electric Service Agreement (“BSA”), Exhibit LKB-2;
                                                                                      I




0   The entire Contribution in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”) Agreement, Exhibit LKB-3; and

0
    Analyses that, far from focusing on the data center Customer, address the Application’s
    projected impacts to other ratepayers, such as Exhibits RDJ-2 and SD-2.


Blocking the NPOS’ client representatives from seeing this information is clearly prejudicial.

Without access to the AEO materials, the client representatives have been unable to thoroughly


review ELL’s ﬁlings. Indeed, due to the breadth of these AEO designations, the client


representatives cannot even review portions of their own direct testimonyprepared by experts

working on their behalf, currently under development and due to be ﬁled July 24, 2026      —
                                                                                                four


days ﬁom now.




       C.   Granting the NPOs.’Motion Would Not Create a Public Disclosure Risk.

       The implication of ELL’s AEO designation, as Well as the Company’s Opposition


argument, is that certain individuals simply cannot be trusted with conﬁdential information. ELL


presents no evidence or argument to support this offensive assertion. The NPOs’ behavior in

Docket No. U-3 7425, Where the client representatives were able to access “Attorney’s Eyes


Only” information, demonstrates that the NPOs treat the conﬁdentiality designation with utmost

seriousness. ELL cannot cite to a single instance in which the NPOs publicly disseminated


conﬁdential material, including AEO designated material, during that proceeding.
           While the NPOs never publicly disclosed any conﬁdential information received in U-'


37425 (or ‘any other case for that matter), the same cannot be said of ELL. Indeed, if the


previous disclosureof conﬁdential material somehow disqualiﬁed a party from continuing to

receive it, then ELL itself would not be handling this material. In Docket No. U-37425, the


Company mistakenly disclosed HSPM information in the public version of its October 30, 2024

initial ﬁling and did not realize that this disclosure‘ had occurred until 51/; months later. During


this time period, the AEO material was available to anyone accessing the public docket.9


          Through their previous participation in proceedings involving commercially sensitive

information, the NPOs have amply demonstrated that they understand and appreciate that this

proceeding involves a great deal of market-sensitive and customer-speciﬁc information and that

this information must be treated with utmost care. Moreover, the NPOs are not in the business of


building energy inﬁastructure or transacting in the computing industry, and can gain no

commercial advantage from seeing the concealed infonnation.” They are not a “competitor or



9
    See Filing Letter from D. Skylar Rosenbloom, ELL, to Ms. Krys Abell, LPSC (April 15, 2025)

(“On October 30, 2024, [ELL] ﬁled the Public Redacted version of the Application of Entergy
‘Louisiana, LLC for Approval of Generation and Transmission Resources in Connection with
Service to a Single Customer for a Project in North Louisiana (‘Application’). It has come to our
attention that there was ‘HSPM’a'esz'gnatea’f0r Attorney's Eyes Only inadvertently left
unredacted. We request that the Direct Testimony of Laura K. Beauchamp (‘Testimony’), in its
entirety please be removed from any digital and/or physical copies of the “Application” and
replaced with the corrected version of the ‘Testimony’ provided with this ﬁling”) (emphasis
added).
1°
     More speciﬁcally, the client representatives do not engage in any activity that the

Conﬁdentiality Agreement at section 2.0 identiﬁes as “present[ing] an unreasonable risk of
harm,” including:

“(i) the marketing or sale of electric power or energy at wholesale, (ii) the purchase or sale of
electric power or energy at wholesale, (iii) the provision of electricity marketing consulting
services to entities engaged in the sale or purchase of electric power. at wholesale; (iv) the pricing
for: the sale of potential electric generation development project facilities or the electric power or

energy thereﬁom, or of potential upgrades or enhancements to such facilities or the electric
power or energy therefrom, with the exception of the development and/ or evaluation of proj ects
for self- or co-generation of electricity; (V) the pricing for competitive bids for purchases, sales,
 staunch business adversary” of Meta (ELL Opp. at 6).          They simply represent their members, and

other concerned ordinary Louisianans.


           ELL’s further argument, that one of the NPOS intentionally disclosed conﬁdential


material in a prior- case, is highly misleading. ELL attempts to draw a distinction between


                   disclosures (like the Company’s disclosure ofAEO material in Docket No. U-
               ”
“inadverten


37425 case), and “intentiona
                                 ”
                                     disclosures (like the one   purportedly -committed by   an NPO in




another case). This is a false distinction. Both disclosures were mistakes, and the disclosure by


the NPO in the other case was- no more “intentional” than ELL’s ﬁling of public testimony that


contained AEO material.” As explained in the attached declaration from Ms. Logan Burke, the


Alliance for Affordable Energy’s Executive Director, the disclosure in 2022 by a former Alliance


employee to an expert was inadvertent, based on that employee’s expectation that e-mail

transmission of the expert’s confidentiality agreement to ELL’s counsel had succeeded. Upon


learning of the error, the Alliance immediately took steps to correct it; the expert did not actually

view the sensitive materialgand the organization also created a new protocol to avoid such errors


and adequately safeguard confidential information in the future.” The Tribunal should reject


this misguided eﬁbrt to impugn the integrity of the NPOS and their representatives.


           The Tribunal should find that ELL7s implication that the NPO client representatives


cannot be trusted with AEO designated material has not been supported by ELL and has no basis


in fact.




or construction of electric transmission      facilities; and (vi) design, construction, or operation of a
data center.”
11
     Moreover, the NPOS’ inadvertent release did not involve the public disclosure of information.
The information was disclosed to an expert who had signed the conﬁdentiality agreement and
that expert deleted the conﬁdential information without opening the document. In contrast, ELL
left conﬁdential information in a public docket for over five months.
12
     See, Declaration of Logan A. Burke. Attachment A.
           D. ELLE: Cavalier Attitude Toward Informing Parties Regarding Which Individuals
              Cannot Receive AEO Designated Information Belies the Importance of this

              Designation

          At the outset, it is   important   to note that ELL is the “gatekeeper” regarding conﬁdential


information. Since ELL solely decides which individuals can receive AEO designated


information, the other parties have no method of determining who can receive such information

unless ELL informs the parties regarding the designations. The Tribunal should be aware that


ELL is not proactive in the least at ensuring that parties know which individuals       are not to
receive AEO designated materials.


          For example, the NPOs and their counsel were not informed which individuals were not



permitted to see AEO designated material until counsel for the NPOs requested a list ﬁ'om ELL
so that   discovery requests could-be appropriately served. Counsel for the NPOs received that list

on June    9, 2026.13 ELL does not dispute that the Motion’s AttachmentA is the list the NPOs

received from ELL.

          The NPOs are disturbed to learn that the AEO designated materials list they received was


incorrect. Attached to ELL’s Opposition is a different list which includes two individuals from


SREA. Until July 17, 2026, when the NPOs received both ELL’s Opposition and SREA’s


comments, the NPOs were unaware that the list they received from ELL was incomplete. ELL


never   provided a correction or otherwise informed the NPOs that the list had changed. To this

day,—the NPOs have never been informed by ELL that the AEO list they have been relying on is




13
     The list the NPOs received is attached to the NPOs’ Motion as Attachment A. It is .the NPOs’
understanding that Commission Staff also had to delay serving the parties until ELL provided the
appropriate list.
 wrong. Apparently, ELL has no process for correctly informingparties regarding which

                                                                                                          I
individuals cannot receive AEO designated information.


          ELL’s cavalier attitude should not go unnoticed by the Tribunal. If the protection of the


AEO designated information ﬁom being reviewed by the listed individuals were so vital, one


would assume that ELL would take at least basic steps to ensure that all     parties know who is     to


receive that information and who is barred from reviewing it.


          Finally, the Tribunal should recognize that the addition of two other individuals does not

impact the arguments presented by the NPOS. The NPOs are still significantly prejudiced by

ELL’s reﬁisal to allow the client representatives to participate as full parties in this proceeding.


and are still being denied their right to counsel.




          E.   The Tribunal Can Direct Modiﬁcation of the Conﬁcientialit-y Agreement.



          ELL notes that employees-of each NPO entity (that is, the client representatives) have


signed ELL’s Conﬁdentiality Agreement and agreed to abide by its terms, which include a

prescription against their access to Attorney’s Eyes Only Information. ELL Opp. at 2-4. All of

that is true. Yet it is important to consider, first, that the client representatives did not conduct an


arm’s—length negotiation, with the leverage that normally attends such     dealings, to arrive at the
terms of the "Conﬁdentiality Agreement. The client representatives signed the agreement because


it was the only option provided by   ELL, the incumbent monopoly utility,     to facilitate their


participation in this proceeding on.behalf of their organizations’ Louisiana members and

supporters.” Moreover, the client representatives have provided due consideration        —
                                                                                             their




14
     See Aguillard v. Auction Management C0r_p., 908 So.2d 1, 8-10 (La. 2005), for a discussion of
the dynamics attendant to “a standard contract, usually in printed form, prepared by a
                                                                                             party of
superior bargaining power for adherence or rejection of the weaker party” (quoting Golz 12.
Children is‘ Bureau ofNew Orleans, 326 So.2d 865, 869 (La. 1976)). In this instance, the NPOS



                                                     10
 commitment to adequately protect conﬁdential      information   —
                                                                    in exchange for ELL’s ﬁirnishing


of conﬁdential information (thus far, only HSPM information) to them, and they will continue


abiding by the contract they .haVe executed.


        While ELL glibly cites “the core tenets of Louisiana contract law,” Opp. at 4, ELL


declines to note that a contract can be amended by mutual consent. La. Civ. Code arts. 1906,


1983. ELL further declines to note that the ConﬁdentialityAgreement, provided as Exhibit 1 to


its Application in this matter, has not been approved by the Commission, and also that the


agreement provides at section 9: “[e]ach party [. .[] shall have the right to seek changes m the
                                                   .




Conﬁdentiality Agreement, as appropriate, from the Commission[.]” In Docket No. U-3 7425,

the NPOs asked ELL multiple times to provide their client representatives access to Attorney’s


Eyes Only information; ELL stonewalled, then declined prior to the NPOS’ ﬁling of a similar

motion in that proceeding. As shown by ELL’s intransigence in its Opposition, attemptsat


negotiating AEO access for the client representatives (as contemplated in sections 9 and 11 of the

ConﬁdentialityAgreement) in the instant matter would have been fruitless. NPOs are not

advancing a “Catch-22” or arguing that “portions of the Conﬁdentiality Agreement do not apply

to them” or seeking to be “exempt ﬁ'0II1 the terms of ‘the Conﬁdentiality Agreement” (ELL Opp.



at 8). NPOS are simplyexercising their contractual right to seek relief from the Agreement’s


onerous terms as   initially written. One accurate point from ELL is that the Conﬁdentiality

Agreement “prevents certain of [NPOs’] designees from obtaining AEO information and they are

asking the Tribunal to relieve them of those constraints.” ELL Opp. at 7.



were not in a   position to bargain regarding the terms of the agreement with ELL and were
required to sign the document prior to receiving any conﬁdential information. ELL clearly was
and still is in a superior bargaining position.




                                                  11
         The Commission has plenary power under Louisiana’s Constitution to regulate all


common carriers and   public utilities, and these authorities “must be construed with practicality

and liberality in order to accomplish their objects and to enable the Commission to perform the


duties required of it by the people.” La. Const. Art. IV § 2l(B); Bowie v. La. Pub. Serv. Comm ’n,

627 So.2d 164, 166 (1993).    Nothing in the Commission’s Rule 12.1 governs the termsof a

utility-intervenor conﬁdentiality agreement or requires that employees of intervenor parties may

not access certain conﬁdential information.15 The Commission should order ELL to
                                                                                 arrange for

the amendment of the definition of “Authorized Persons” in the Conﬁdentiality Agreement to


provide for AEO access by employees of “Reviewing Parties” (as deﬁned in that agreement).

The NPO client representatives stand ready to provide appropriate consideration     —


                                                                                        carefully

safeguarding such AEO materials and information       —
                                                          in exchange.




                                          CONCLUSION


       For the foregoing reasons, and the reasons explained in the NPOS’ Motion, the


Commission should find that the NPOS’ client representatives are. entitled to review the AEO


designated material, and order ELL to immediately provide those client representatives With

access to such material.



       CONTINUED FOR SIGNATURE


                                                                             I




15
  Commission Rule 12.1 provides that “Upon request of a regulated entity...
                                                                            any records
received by the Commission which are shown by the company. .and found by the Commission
                                                                    .




to be trade secret, proprietary, or conﬁdential information. .shall be kept confidential and shall
                                                               .




be exempt ﬁom public disclosure.”      Thus, ELL’s Conﬁdentiality Agreement exceeds the scope of
restrictions set forth in the Rule. The Rule provides that conﬁdential documents will be
                                                                                       exempt
ﬁom public disclosure, not that the documents will be exempt from disclosure to the parties.
